opus-5.5.text:
I think I was very lucky. My advisors at MIT gave me an unusual combination of trust and support. On the technical side, they let me go deep into things that, at the time, didn't look like a typical graphics PhD. Building a programming language and compiler like Taichi is a huge engineering investment. It's risky, and it doesn't always map neatly onto a paper-per-year rhythm. Many advisors would have said, "That's interesting, but let's focus on something more publishable." Mine didn't. They let me own the direction.

But independence doesn't mean being left alone. The support showed up in other ways. They asked the right high-level questions. Why does this matter? Who's going to use it? What's the core insight beyond the engineering? Those questions forced me to articulate the research contribution, not just build a cool system. They also helped a lot with the less visible parts of research, like how to write a paper so reviewers understand it, how to present work, and how to think about a career. And they protected the time and freedom I needed to do something long-term.

Looking back, I'd describe it like this: they gave me a lot of rope, but they were always there if I started to fall. As a student, especially one who likes to build things, that's probably the best environment you can ask for. You learn to take responsibility for your own direction, and that's what you really need after the PhD, whether you go into academia or start a company.

r001.rationale: The response describes trust, support, and protected time, but does not say their help was disproportionate to the limited time spent meeting.

r002.rationale: It says the advisors let Hu own the direction and asked high-level research questions, while allowing him to choose and pursue the technical work without prescribing its specifics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I was very lucky with my advisor, Fredo Durand at MIT. Looking back, the thing I appreciate most is that he gave me a lot of room, and the room came with real support rather than neglect, which is a rare combination.

When I started working on Taichi, it wasn't an obvious thesis topic. It was a programming language and a compiler, in a graphics group. A lot of advisors would have steered me back toward something more clearly publishable in their own area. Fredo didn't. He asked hard questions about why it mattered and who would use it, but once I had answers, he let me go build it. That meant I spent long stretches writing infrastructure, which doesn't produce papers quickly, and he was patient with that.

The support showed up in a few concrete ways. One was taste. He had a very good sense for what makes a result compelling, and he would push me on framing, on experiments, on what the actual contribution was versus what I was excited about. Those conversations shaped the papers a lot more than they shaped the code. Another was connecting me with people. Several collaborations came from him pointing me at someone and saying, you two should talk. And honestly, a big part of it was just believing it would work when I wasn't sure myself.

Technically, though, he mostly stayed out of the way. I think he understood that for systems work you need one person holding the whole design in their head, and that person has to be the student. If he had been dictating the architecture, Taichi would have been a worse project and I would have learned less.

So my assessment is that he got the balance right. The independence forced me to grow up as a researcher, and the support meant that independence didn't turn into isolation. When I later started a company around Taichi, a lot of how I try to work with my own team comes directly from that experience: set the direction and the bar together, then trust people with the details.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the advisor as supportive and patient but does not mention how often or how long they met, or say the help was significant relative to limited meeting time.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the advisor asked hard questions about why the project mattered and who would use it, then let Hu build it; technically, he mostly stayed out of the way and did not dictate the architecture.
